transcript: Meeting header: 2026-12-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48 mins | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE), Jonah Rivera (Redwood SE), Emily Chen (Veridian Head of Platform), Mark D'Souza (SRE), Priya Rao (CTO)

Summary: Initial discovery focusing on availability tiers, SLA targets, and tradeoffs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Customer cares about predictable p99 latency, data residency in EU, and a low error budget for chat flows. Exploring warm standby and region steering options, plus who operates fallbacks.
Topics: availability tiers, warm vs cold standby, multi-region routing, KV cache consistency across regions, SLA math and error budgets, private/VPC constraints, security/compliance
Questions: Who owns failover? What are typical RTO/RPO with Redwood Dedicated? How does KV cache warmup affect tail latency?
[00:00] Alice Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros? We're from Redwood, I'm Alice in AE, this is Jonah on the SE side.
[00:12] Emily Chen: Hi, Emily here. I'm the platform lead at Veridian. We run customer facing AI assistants in EU and NA, looking at reliability and costs.
[00:20] Priya Rao: Priya, CTO, focused on availability requirements and regulatory constraints. Short on time so we'll jump to constraints after backlog summary.
[00:30] Jonah Rivera: Great — do you want to start with your SLO targets and where you're currently seeing issues?

[00:36] Mark D'Souza: Sure. We aim for 99.95% in production for inference endpoints, p99 under 600ms for prompt to first token in EU. Lately tails spike during morning peaks and after deploys — we've had a couple 15–30 min blips.
[00:51] Alice Park: 99.95% is tight. That's about 22 minutes of downtime per month, so we'll have to think about fallbacks and error budgets. Are you running models in-house today?

[01:03] Emily Chen: We have an in-house serving layer but it's getting expensive and operationally heavy. That's why we're evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private — we'd like the predictability of Dedicated but worried about cost and data residency for EU PII.

[01:22] Jonah Rivera: Understood. High level tradeoffs: Hosted gives lowest onboarding but less isolation; Dedicated gives reserved capacity and predictable latency; Private gives you the VPC/control plane for compliance. We can talk about warm standby across regions for Dedicated/Private to hit that 99.95% SLA.
[01:41] Mark D'Souza: When you say warm standby, how warm? Do we pre-warm KV cache across regions? That cache is big, and the cold start penalty kills p99.

[01:52] Jonah Rivera: Good point. We do prefix and KV cache replication strategies. Two common patterns: 1) active-active KV with async cross-region replication — low RPO but possible inconsistency at edge; 2) active-passive with proactive cache prewarming in standby region — more control but increased cost. We can show benchmarks.
[02:11] Emily Chen: Active-active sounds risky for consistency — our assistants need a consistent persona state. What's the typical inconsistency window?

[02:18] Jonah Rivera: It depends on your replication pipeline, typically seconds to a few minutes if you're async. For strict consistency you might prefer region-local writes with inter-region sync, or use a single writer with read replicas. There's a cost/latency tradeoff.

[02:33] Alice Park: Also worth noting fallback policy options: we can route to a smaller/cheaper model variant on capacity issues, or return degraded responses with a flag, or fall back to cached responses. Which is preferable for you?
[02:46] Priya Rao: Degraded responses are acceptable only if labeled. We can't silently change output quality. Also audit logs must show fallback events. SOC2 auditability is non-negotiable.

[02:56] Jonah Rivera: We have per-request tracing and token-level cost/latency logs in Redwood Console. Fallbacks are annotated and there are hooks to route to an alternate model and to log reason codes. We'll share examples.
[03:10] Mark D'Souza: For SLA math — if we do Dedicated with two regions and active-active routing, what are typical RTO/RPO?

[03:18] Jonah Rivera: With warm standby and health-check based failover, RTOs in low single-digit minutes are achievable; RPO depends on replication choice. If you accept eventual consistency, you can get near-zero RPO for many cases via async replication with fast commit; strict RPO zero requires synchronous cross-region replication which impacts latency.
[03:36] Emily Chen: How do we measure p99 improvements vs cost? We need a simple model: baseline cost, +warm standby, +cross-region sync. Can you provide a spreadsheet?
[03:46] Alice Park: Yes, we'll send a cost model with three scenarios. Also include expected p99 tail improvements and token cost deltas.

[03:55] Jonah Rivera: Quick note on routing: smart routing policy can route by latency (closest region), by cost (fallback to cheaper region/model), or by customer tier. You can also do region steering with sticky session behavior. That might help during partial outages.
[04:10] Mark D'Souza: For partial outages we want circuit breakers at the call layer so we don't overwhelm downstream when a region is flapping. Does Redwood have built-in circuit breaker support?

[04:19] Jonah Rivera: We surface circuit breaker metrics and can enforce client-side throttles; the runtime supports token budget limits and backpressure. You can set route-level SLOs and automatic fallback rules. It's configurable in the control plane.
[04:31] Emily Chen: How about private deployment in our VPC? We need to know whether Redwood or Veridian owns failover orchestration — ops ownership question.

[04:40] Alice Park: For Private, customer typically owns the infra failover but we provide the control plane and playbooks. For Dedicated, Redwood can operate failover per the SLA or hand off to customer ops under a managed contract. We'll document ownership models.
[04:55] Priya Rao: Security: KMS integration for key rotation and HSM for certain keys, plus audit logs — can you confirm flow?

[05:04] Jonah Rivera: Yes. We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, customer HSM). Keys for model artifacts and tokenization can be customer-managed. We'll attach the network diagram and KMS spec.
[05:16] Mark D'Souza: Any concerns with EU data residency and cross-border cache replication? We may need to avoid moving certain PII out of region.

[05:24] Alice Park: In that case Private or Dedicated with region pinning is the safer path — you can pin EU traffic to EU-only nodes, and for things that must stay in EU we keep logs and KV local. We also support audit controls and retention policies.
[05:36] Emily Chen: On fallback triggers: do you recommend latency threshold or error rate? And should we prefer model fallback or regional failover first?

[05:44] Jonah Rivera: We typically recommend layered triggers: immediate local model fallback on response time threshold (e.g., if 95th latency exceeds x), then route to another region if error budgets exceed threshold. That avoids cross-region hops for transient spikes. Also per-route policies let you prefer model variant fallback before region failover.
[05:59] Alice Park: Operationally it's useful to have a canary window for deploys with automatic rollback if tail latency increases — do you do canaries?

[06:05] Jonah Rivera: Yes, Redwood supports canary and percentage rollouts with automatic fallback. You can set watch thresholds on p95/p99 and token quality regressions. We'll show the rollout UI in the next demo.
[06:15] Mark D'Souza: About benchmarking: will Redwood run a bench on our model or do we bring it? We want to simulate warm-cache and cold-cache tails.

[06:23] Jonah Rivera: We can run benchmarks with your model artifact in a sandbox or you can bring a representative trace. Best is to provide a small test model or weights and a traffic file; we'll simulate both cold and warm cache scenarios and show p50/p95/p99.
[06:35] Emily Chen: Timeline — we want to be production-ready for a limited pilot by end of Q1. Is that feasible?
[06:41] Alice Park: Yes, pilot in Q1 is reasonable. Typical path: discovery -> pilot (4–8 weeks) -> expand to Dedicated or Private. We'll scope the pilot to a small set of endpoints and SLOs.
[06:50] Priya Rao: Pricing: we need predictable capacity numbers. If we commit to a Dedicated pool, can we get a burst buffer for unexpected traffic?

[06:58] Alice Park: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. We can include burst commitments in the contract for an additional buffer. We'll outline options in the pricing doc.
[07:08] Mark D'Souza: One worry: failover flapping causing double charges or duplicate processing. How do you prevent duplicate inference when failover happens?

[07:17] Jonah Rivera: Good call. We provide idempotency tokens and request dedupe in the front-door. Also, KV cache coordination includes version stamps to avoid double application. We'll detail mechanisms in a follow-up note.
[07:29] Emily Chen: For auditability and for our SOC2, we need visible logs for fallback events and who triggered them. Can Redwood tag fallback events to external incident systems?
[07:37] Jonah Rivera: Yes, webhook integrations to PagerDuty/Datadog are supported, plus event streams to your SIEM. Fallback events have reason codes and context.
[07:46] Alice Park: Quick note — competitors question: are you evaluating any others?

[07:50] Emily Chen: We're talking to Anthropic and a few consulting shops for an in-house rewrite. Anthropic is strong on model access, but we're leaning toward a provider that gives better operational guarantees.
[07:59] Mark D'Souza: Also looking at a hybrid approach — keep critical flows on our infra, move burst/low-sensitivity routes to Redwood Hosted.
[08:07] Jonah Rivera: That hybrid is common — you can route by route and tag sensitive routes to Dedicated/Private. Hybrid routing reduces cost and keeps control.

[08:15] Emily Chen: Can you show an example of a fallback policy configuration? We want to see rules like: if p95>400ms for 5m, downgrade to smaller model; if error rate >1% for 2m, route to EU warm-standby region.
[08:25] Jonah Rivera: We'll include a sample policy in the follow-up. The control plane supports time windows, thresholds, and prioritized actions.

[08:33] Alice Park: Next steps recap — we'll send pricing and pilot plan. Jonah will prepare a bench plan and sample fallback policy. Emily/Mark will share traffic traces and constraints. Any questions before we wrap?
[08:42] Priya Rao: One last — does Redwood do post-incident RCA support if we sign an enterprise package?
[08:47] Alice Park: Yes, enterprise includes post-incident support, joint runbooks, and a named CSM/SE. We'll outline the tiers.
[08:55] Emily Chen: Great. Thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity. We'll look for the docs.
[08:59] Alice Park: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials. End call.

Transcript notes: transcription contains minor mis-hearings (e.g., 'K-V cache' vs KV cache, 'Anthropic' sometimes muffled). There are occasional speaker attribution differences consistent with Fireflies exports.
